LEF-JEPA: Denoising-Trained Latent Energy Fields for Spatial Representation Learning

Zhiyuan Liu    Zhihao Xu    Sicheng Liu    Huanhuan Huang Affiliation: Qinous Technology Co., Ltd  Tsinghua University
Abstract

A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) that applies prediction supervision only at masked positions struggles to clearly capture object shapes and boundaries in its latent representations. We further observe that some existing methods improve spatial structure while also retaining rich variations in texture and color. However, preserving more low-level visual information does not necessarily make representations better suited to prediction and action. This raises a key question: how can we strengthen the spatial structure in latent representations that supports prediction and action without over-encoding these details? We introduce LEF-JEPA, which learns spatial structure through target-guided latent recovery and transfers this supervision to the visual encoder through a relative-energy constraint; the energy module is used only during pretraining and adds no inference overhead. To reduce the cost of energy optimization during pretraining, we further construct a conditional Ising Hamiltonian that allows low-energy-state search to be performed by specialized Ising solvers. On physical hardware, we validate the feasibility of achieving lower forward latency with fewer local updates. Under a unified CIFAR-10 pretraining and frozen-encoder evaluation protocol, both realizations outperform V-JEPA2.1 in image classification, foreground segmentation, and visual planning.

1 Introduction

Visual world models need to preserve the scene geometry required for prediction and action. The Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) uses features extracted by an encoder as prediction targets without encoding every pixel-level detail in the observation [21, 9]. As JEPA applications extend from image-level recognition to pixel-level scene parsing and action-conditioned planning [23, 4, 26, 24, 27], high-level semantics alone no longer suffice: segmentation requires clear object boundaries, while planning depends on spatial layout and relations among objects. Visual encoders must therefore preserve the local spatial structure required for prediction and action while forming high-level semantics.

However, when predictive supervision is applied only to masked positions, JEPA struggles to clearly capture object shapes and boundaries in latent representations [23]. The V-JEPA2 features in Figure (a) form coarse regions in which object contours and internal parts are weakly distinguished. V-JEPA2.1 strengthens dense prediction and multi-level self-supervision to improve the representation of spatial structure [23]. We further observe that this improvement is accompanied by rich texture and color variations: the local-roughness responses in Figure (b) are broadly distributed across object interiors and backgrounds. Preserving more appearance detail does not necessarily make representations better suited to prediction and action. The key question is therefore how to strengthen the spatial structure in latent representations that supports prediction and action without requiring detailed encoding of low-level visual information.

We use spatial-structure cues in multi-level target representations to guide the local recovery of perturbed latent representations. However, even if the recovered representations capture these cues, the visual encoder’s direct outputs may not retain the corresponding spatial information. Because downstream tasks directly use encoder representations, the supervision provided by the recovery process must be transferred to the encoder during pretraining, so that downstream tasks do not depend on iterative recovery at test time [12].

Accordingly, we introduce LEF-JEPA, which augments masked prediction with target-guided latent energy learning. It uses multi-level targets to learn local recovery directions for perturbed representations and transfers this structural supervision to the visual encoder through a relative-energy constraint. The two training paths are decoupled, so encoder updates do not backpropagate through the multi-step recovery process; the energy module is used only during pretraining and therefore adds no downstream inference overhead.

To explore more efficient energy learning during pretraining, we further construct a conditional Ising Hamiltonian that enables LEF-JEPA to interface with specialized Ising solvers. Unlike prior work that primarily uses physical Ising devices for sampling in generative models [8, 30], we incorporate physical low-energy-state search into self-supervised pretraining and validate this closed-loop training process on a physical photonic coherent Ising machine (CIM).

We conduct self-supervised pretraining on CIFAR-10 [18] and freeze the encoders for image classification, out-of-distribution transfer to PartImageNet [13] foreground segmentation, and Two-Room visual planning. Across ViT-S and ViT-B, LEF-JEPA breaks the observed tradeoff between semantic and spatial capability. The continuous neural field achieves the strongest ViT-S foreground segmentation, whereas the Ising realization solved on a physical CIM requires only a single local update step (K=1K=1) and lower pretraining latency while attaining the strongest classification and visual planning results at both scales, together with the strongest ViT-B foreground segmentation.

The contributions of this work are:

  • •

    Target-guided latent energy field: Using structural cues from multi-level targets to learn local recovery directions for perturbed representations. The energy field is used only during pretraining and adds no inference overhead.

  • •

    Decoupled dual-path energy training: Sharing one energy function while updating the energy field and encoder separately. The encoder receives supervision through a one-sided relative-energy constraint without backpropagating through multi-step recovery.

  • •

    Hardware-accelerated Ising realization: Formulating a conditional Ising Hamiltonian compatible with specialized Ising quantum hardware and validating the closed training loop on a physical CIM, using a single update to accelerate and improve self-supervised representation learning.

2 Related Work

2.1 Latent Prediction and Spatial Representation Learning

I-JEPA uses visible regions within a single image to predict features of masked regions [3]; V-JEPA extends this task to video, using spatiotemporal context to predict features of masked video blocks [7]. V-JEPA2 extends this paradigm to an action-conditioned world model for visual planning, establishing a common foundation for recognition and control [4]. Causal-JEPA uses object-level latent masking to learn interaction-dependent object dynamics [24], while Temporal Straightening constrains latent-trajectory curvature to make the representation geometry better suited to planning [27]. Together, these works show that representations for prediction and action should not only preserve spatial structure, but also emphasize information relevant to interactions and dynamics rather than indiscriminately encoding all low-level visual information in the observations.

Recent work designs training constraints around local features and their spatial relations to improve performance on tasks such as segmentation and depth estimation. V-JEPA2.1 supervises both visible and masked tokens at multiple encoder depths [23]. Because it likewise uses multi-level targets but applies supervision through direct regression, it provides the closest regression-based counterpart to the energy formulation of LEF-JEPA. DINOv3, meanwhile, introduces Gram anchoring to preserve pairwise similarities among local features over long training schedules [25]. Together, these approaches strengthen the encoder’s ability to extract structured spatial information from pixel observations, showing that local spatial relations benefit from constraints beyond standard masked prediction. Another line of work regularizes global consistency and distributional shape in latent representations. LeVJEPA combines global–local video-view consistency with SIGReg, allowing semantically organized regions to emerge even though the loss reads only clip-level embeddings [19]. VISReg decouples embedding scale from distributional shape through variance and Sliced-Wasserstein constraints  [28]. Explicit geometric information can also serve as pretraining supervision: LingBot-Vision uses online subpixel boundary detection to guide masked prediction  [11]. Unlike explicit boundary detection or dense token regression, LEF-JEPA uses multi-level target representations to supervise a conditional energy field in learning local recovery directions for perturbed representations, then transfers the supervision provided by recovery to the visual encoder through a one-sided relative-energy constraint.

2.2 Energy Learning and Physical Ising Solvers

Energy-based models (EBMs) formulate inference and prediction as the search for low-energy configurations [22]. This principle has been applied to state-space trajectory planning [10], token-level associative-memory updates in Energy Transformer [14], and iterative test-time refinement of candidate predictions in Energy-Based Transformers [12]. Within JEPA-based representation learning, EB-JEPA defines latent prediction error itself as energy and combines it with VICReg [6] or SIGReg [5] to avoid representation collapse [26]. LEF-JEPA does not redefine the prediction loss as energy or require iterative gradient descent at inference. It retains standard masked prediction and introduces an auxiliary conditional energy mechanism only during pretraining. The energy-field objective learns local recovery directions guided by multi-level targets, while the one-sided relative-energy constraint transfers this supervision to the visual encoder without backpropagating through the multi-step recovery process during encoder updates.

Beyond direct parameterization by continuous neural networks, conditional energy landscapes can also be constructed with discrete spin models. The central challenge is to search low-energy states efficiently and convert them into training gradients. Neural Boltzmann Machines, for example, generate the parameters of a restricted Boltzmann model from context and analytically marginalize hidden units to obtain conditional free energy, yet still rely on Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling on classical architectures to estimate generative-likelihood gradients [20]. To overcome the efficiency bottleneck of software sampling, specialized physical Ising solvers—including superconducting quantum annealers such as D-Wave that exploit quantum tunneling [17, 16] and coherent Ising machines (CIMs) based on coupled optical oscillators  [15, 29]—use the natural evolution of physical systems for high-speed search over low-energy spin configurations. Existing machine-learning studies that employ physical Ising hardware, whether through quantum-annealing sampling [1, 2] or noise-injected optoelectronic sampling [8], primarily treat it as a Boltzmann sampler for estimating negative-phase statistics in generative models and do not directly turn discrete hardware samples into gradients with respect to continuous visual representations. LEF-JEPA instead extends physical Ising solving from generative-likelihood estimation to self-supervised visual representation learning. Its conditional Ising Hamiltonian incorporates low-energy-state search into pretraining, allowing specialized Ising solvers to participate in latent-space energy learning.

3 Method

LEF-JEPA augments masked latent prediction with target-guided conditional energy learning over visible tokens. To endow the visual encoder with spatial coherence without iterative correction at inference, two complementary processes are connected through a shared energy function. The Energy Field Loss (ℒfield\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{field}}) supervises local correction displacements of perturbed representations to shape the energy landscape. The Encoder Energy Loss (ℒenc\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{enc}}) encourages online representations to lie below the energy of a multi-level target reference, so that the learned structure is reflected in encoder representations. The objectives share the energy function, but their gradients follow strictly separated parameter paths. Figure 2 summarizes the complete framework.

3.1 Masked Latent Prediction

Let Ω=V∪M\Omega=V\cup M denote the visible and masked patch-position sets of image xx. The online encoder fθf_{\theta} encodes the visible patches xVx_{V}, while the masked predictor pψp_{\psi} predicts latent representations at the masked positions MM. The target encoder fθ¯f_{\bar{\theta}} processes the unmasked view to provide supervision; its parameters are updated by an exponential moving average (EMA) of the online encoder and receive no gradients. With zj⋆z_{j}^{\star} denoting a target patch token, the Masked Prediction Loss is

ℒpred=1|M|​D​∑j∈M‖pψ​(fθ​(xV))j−sg⁡(zj⋆)‖1\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}=\frac{1}{|M|D}\sum_{j\in M}\left\|p_{\psi}(f_{\theta}(x_{V}))_{j}-\operatorname{sg}(z_{j}^{\star})\right\|_{1} (1)

3.2 Target-Guided Spatial Objects

To model spatial relations among visible patches, we construct three representations over VV: candidate states SS to be corrected, contextual conditions CC, and a multi-level target reference TT. The visible positions are partitioned into disjoint candidate and anchor sets QQ and AA, with V=Q∪˙AV=Q\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}A and Q∩A=∅Q\cap A=\varnothing. These sets select SS and CC from the online encoder and TT from the target encoder.

A central requirement is that the energy remain sensitive to relative spatial variation across patches while keeping feature scale calibrated. Standard token-wise normalization removes relative magnitude differences between object boundaries and interior regions. We instead use contrast-preserving spatial normalization. Given the nn patch tokens of one image, H=[h1,…,hn]∈ℝn×DH=[h_{1},\ldots,h_{n}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times D}, we subtract the spatial mean μ⁡(H)\mu(H) to remove the component shared by the full image, then scale all tokens by a single RMS factor computed jointly over positions and channels:

𝒩s​(H)=H−μ⁡(H)1n​D​‖H−μ⁡(H)‖F2+ϵ,μ⁡(H)=1n​∑jhj\mathcal{N}_{s}(H)=\frac{H-\mu(H)}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{nD}\|H-\mu(H)\|_{F}^{2}+\epsilon}},\quad\mu(H)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j}h_{j} (2)

All positions share this RMS scalar, preserving their relative spatial salience. For a transformer of depth LL with selected intermediate layers ℓ1,ℓ2\ell_{1},\ell_{2}, the clean online candidate source and multi-level anchor condition are

S=𝒩s​(Hθ(L))Q,C={𝒩s​(Hθ(ℓ1))A,𝒩s​(Hθ(ℓ2))A}S=\mathcal{N}_{s}(H_{\theta}^{(L)})_{Q},\qquad C=\left\{\mathcal{N}_{s}(H_{\theta}^{(\ell_{1})})_{A},\mathcal{N}_{s}(H_{\theta}^{(\ell_{2})})_{A}\right\} (3)

To make TT combine mid-level geometry with high-level semantics, let ℐ\mathcal{I} denote the selected target-encoder layers and wℓw_{\ell} their fusion weights. Each layer is spatially normalized over VV to align feature scales across depths; the layers are then fused, normalized again, and restricted to the candidate positions QQ:

T=𝒩s​(∑ℓ∈ℐwℓ​𝒩s​(Hθ¯,V(ℓ)))|Q,∑ℓwℓ=1T=\left.\mathcal{N}_{s}\!\left(\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{I}}w_{\ell}\mathcal{N}_{s}(H_{\bar{\theta},V}^{(\ell)})\right)\right|_{Q},\quad\sum_{\ell}w_{\ell}=1 (4)

Here, CC conditions Eϕ​(C,q)E_{\phi}(C,q), while TT supervises ℒfield\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{field}} and provides the reference state in ℒenc\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{enc}}.

3.3 Learning a Reachable Latent Energy Field

For the neural energy parameterization, a Conditional Energy Transformer parameterizes the scalar energy Eϕ​(C,q)∈ℝE_{\phi}(C,q)\in\mathbb{R}. Self-attention models interactions among candidate states in QQ, while cross-attention conditions them on the multi-level anchors in CC. A token-wise linear head shared across positions maps each contextualized candidate token hih_{i} to a local contribution eie_{i}, which are summed to obtain

Eϕ​(C,q)=∑ieiE_{\phi}(C,q)=\sum_{i}e_{i} (5)

To shape the local landscape around the data manifold, the clean candidate representation SS is perturbed by scale-preserving Gaussian corruption:

q0=1−σ2​S+σ​ε,ε∼𝒩⁡(0,I)q_{0}=\sqrt{1-\sigma^{2}}\,S+\sigma\varepsilon,\qquad\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) (6)

where σ\sigma denotes the corruption magnitude. Starting from q0q_{0}, we perform KK clipped descent updates on the energy surface,

gk=∇qkEϕ​(C,qk),qk+1=qk−α​𝒞τ​(gk),g_{k}=\nabla_{q_{k}}E_{\phi}(C,q_{k}),\qquad q_{k+1}=q_{k}-\alpha\,\mathcal{C}_{\tau}(g_{k}), (7)

where 𝒞τ\mathcal{C}_{\tau} clips the gradient RMS of each sample to at most τ\tau, limiting the RMS displacement of one update to α​τ\alpha\tau. Let Δ=sg⁡(T−q0)\Delta=\operatorname{sg}(T-q_{0}) be the ideal recovery vector, r=RMS⁡(Δ)r=\operatorname{RMS}(\Delta) its distance, and U=Δ/(r+ϵ)U=\Delta/(r+\epsilon) its RMS-normalized direction.

Requiring qKq_{K} to reach TT within KK steps would demand a per-step RMS of r/Kr/K. Under stronger corruption, r/Kr/K may exceed the distance attainable by a clipped update and would therefore distort the desired energy gradient. We use a reachable-displacement schedule that restricts the supervised step size to a fraction β∈(0,1]\beta\in(0,1] of the maximum update:

ρ=min⁡(rK,β​α​τ),Dk=k​ρ​U\rho=\min\!\left(\frac{r}{K},\,\beta\alpha\tau\right),\qquad D_{k}=k\rho U (8)

If the required per-step displacement r/Kr/K does not exceed the permitted supervised step size β​α​τ\beta\alpha\tau, the cumulative supervised displacement at step KK covers the full recovery path from q0q_{0} to TT; otherwise, each step uses the maximum permitted magnitude and constructs the supervised displacement along the direction from q0q_{0} toward TT. The Energy Field Loss matches the cumulative displacement induced by the energy updates, qk−q0q_{k}-q_{0}, to DkD_{k}:

ℒfield=1∑k=1Kak​∑k=1Kak​‖(qk−q0)−Dk‖Q2|Q|​D\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{field}}=\frac{1}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}a_{k}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}a_{k}\frac{\|(q_{k}-q_{0})-D_{k}\|_{Q}^{2}}{|Q|D} (9)

Supervising cumulative displacement rather than absolute state trains the energy field to point toward TT at each step without requiring an intermediate qkq_{k} to equal the target. Both SS and CC are stop-gradient inputs in ℒfield\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{field}}, so this path updates only the energy parameters ϕ\phi. Because each updated state qkq_{k} depends on ∇qE\nabla_{q}E, optimizing ℒfield\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{field}} requires backpropagating through these energy-gradient updates and therefore involves mixed second-order derivatives with respect to the state and energy parameters; automatic differentiation computes only the required Hessian–vector products without explicitly forming the full Hessian.

3.4 Relative-Energy Supervision for the Encoder

The visual encoder must translate the learned structural preference into its feed-forward representations so that its output SS already occupies a coherent low-energy region. Minimizing Eϕ​(C,S)E_{\phi}(C,S) in isolation provides no sample-specific reference and admits trivial collapse of the energy scale. Because the multi-level target TT represents an uncorrupted, structurally coherent configuration under the same context CC, LEF-JEPA evaluates SS and TT with the same energy function and uses the target energy as a sample-specific comparison reference. Let E¯​(C,X)=E⁡(C,X)/|Q|\bar{E}(C,X)=E(C,X)/|Q| denote energy normalized by the number of candidate positions. A smooth one-sided objective defines the Encoder Energy Loss:

ℒenc=γ​softplus⁡(E¯ϕ​(sg⁡(C),S)−sg⁡[E¯ϕ​(C,T)]γ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{enc}}=\gamma\,\operatorname{softplus}\!\left(\frac{\bar{E}_{\phi}(\operatorname{sg}(C),S)-\operatorname{sg}[\bar{E}_{\phi}(C,T)]}{\gamma}\right) (10)

Here, γ>0\gamma>0 controls the smoothness of the penalty. The softplus places the strongest pressure on positive relative-energy gaps and progressively attenuates once E¯ϕ​(C,S)\bar{E}_{\phi}(C,S) falls below E¯ϕ​(C,T)\bar{E}_{\phi}(C,T). It neither forces S=TS=T nor requires the two scalar energies to match; instead, it constrains SS to the low-energy side defined by the target reference. In ℒenc\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{enc}}, the energy parameters, the explicit anchor condition CC, and the target representation TT are stop-gradient. The loss updates the visual encoder through SS, without differentiating through the KK-step recovery process. Since SS is normalized using statistics shared across all visible tokens, the resulting encoder gradient remains spatially coupled across visible positions.

The parameter-specific objectives are

minθ,ψ⁡ℒpred+λenc​ℒenc,minϕ⁡λfield​ℒfield\min_{\theta,\psi}\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{enc}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{enc}},\qquad\min_{\phi}\;\lambda_{\mathrm{field}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{field}} (11)

where λenc\lambda_{\mathrm{enc}} balances the encoder energy constraint with the masked-prediction objective; after pretraining, the auxiliary energy module is discarded entirely.

3.5 Conditional Ising Energy for Specialized Ising Solvers

This Hamiltonian form is natively compatible with specialized Ising solvers, including superconducting quantum annealers and coherent Ising machines. In this work, we integrate a physical coherent Ising machine (CIM) into the closed training loop to solve hardware-compatible Hamiltonians and return a pool 𝒮\mathcal{S} of low-energy states. A coefficient network maps (C,q)(C,q) to unary biases hi​(C,q)h_{i}(C,q) and symmetric pairwise couplings Ji​j​(C,q)=Jj​i​(C,q)J_{ij}(C,q)=J_{ji}(C,q) with zero diagonal, defining a Hamiltonian over B=16B=16 logical binary spins:

ℋω(s;C,q)=−∑i=1Bhisi−12∑i≠jJi​jsisj,si∈{−1,+1}\mathcal{H}_{\omega}(s;C,q)=-\sum_{i=1}^{B}h_{i}s_{i}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\neq j}J_{ij}s_{i}s_{j},\quad s_{i}\in\{-1,+1\} (12)

Each forward evaluation connects discrete physical search with continuous backpropagation in four stages: (i) a classical network predicts continuous coefficients (h,J)(h,J); (ii) the photonic CIM searches the quantized Hamiltonian and returns a compact pool 𝒮\mathcal{S} of low-energy spin configurations; (iii) the discrete states are rescored by the original, differentiable coefficients; and (iv) a truncated soft minimum aggregates the pool into a smooth conditional scalar energy,

EωIsing(C,q)=−τslog[1|𝒮|∑s∈𝒮exp[−ℋω(s;C,q)/τs]]E_{\omega}^{\mathrm{Ising}}(C,q)=-\tau_{s}\log\!\left[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\exp\!\left[-\mathcal{H}_{\omega}(s;C,q)/\tau_{s}\right]\right] (13)

During differentiation, each s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} is held fixed as a structural anchor, while gradients propagate through (h,J)(h,J) to the latent representation qq. Aggregating the low-energy pool in Eq. (13) smooths changes between competing low-energy configurations.

Within a trajectory of KK energy updates, the physical CIM is queried only at the initial perturbed state q0q_{0}; the returned pool 𝒮\mathcal{S} is reused for all KK local updates. The number of physical calls is therefore 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) with respect to KK. For ℒenc\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{enc}}, separate low-energy pools are queried for SS and TT, and their energies are compared through Eq. (10). The photonic solver thus supplies global discrete low-energy candidates that enter self-supervised representation learning through differentiable rescoring.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Settings

Unified pretraining setup and energy realizations.

To compare architectures under matched conditions, all methods pretrain their visual encoders from scratch with self-supervision on unlabeled CIFAR-10  [18]. Despite the 32×3232\times 32 input resolution, we use 2×22\times 2 patches, producing a dense 16×1616\times 16 spatial token grid (256 tokens per image) that provides fine-grained spatial sampling for modeling object contours and local structure. We evaluate two realizations of our framework: LEF-JEPA with neural scalar energy, and LEF-JEPA-CIM with a conditional Ising Hamiltonian solved by a physical photonic CIM. For each energy realization, KK and λenc\lambda_{\mathrm{enc}} are selected according to linear-classification accuracy on a fixed 5,000-image validation subset of the CIFAR-10 training split and then fixed for all subsequent downstream evaluations. Hardware specifications, quantization protocol, solver timing, and hyperparameter-selection details are provided in the supplementary material.

Frozen-encoder evaluation at three task granularities. After pretraining, each visual encoder is frozen and evaluated at three levels. CIFAR-10 linear classification measures in-distribution global semantics and reports top-1 accuracy. Out-of-distribution dense transfer to PartImageNet  [13] trains a linear foreground-segmentation head on frozen patch tokens and reports foreground IoU. Action-conditioned spatial planning is evaluated through goal-reaching trajectories in the continuous Two-Room environment.

4.2 Joint Semantic and Spatial Gains

Latent organization and cross-task generalization.

Table 1 shows that on ViT-S, V-JEPA2.1 improves foreground IoU over V-JEPA2 by 11.7611.76 points but reduces classification accuracy and planning success by 5.415.41 and 1212 points; EB-JEPA likewise improves segmentation while lowering classification. With frozen encoders and matched task heads, both LEF realizations outperform these baselines across both backbones and all three tasks. On ViT-B, for example, LEF-JEPA improves classification accuracy, foreground IoU, and planning success over V-JEPA2.1 by 3.403.40, 3.973.97, and 77 points, respectively.

Spatial representations and task visualizations.

Patch-token PCA in Figure 3 shows that LEF-JEPA preserves clearer contours and internal structure than V-JEPA2; compared with V-JEPA2.1, it responds less to local texture and color variations and forms more coherent object regions. The out-of-distribution PartImageNet samples exhibit more complete foreground masks, with fewer spills and holes around narrow structures (Figure 4); in the shown Two-Room trajectories, both LEF realizations pass through the doorway and reach the goal region (Figure 5).

Neural-energy and physical-Ising realizations. As shown in Table 1, the two realizations shape representation geometry in fundamentally different ways through a continuous gradient field and a discrete-spin Hamiltonian. In continuous latent space, LEF-JEPA accumulates local recovery displacements through iterative descent (K=3K=3). This fine-grained continuous guidance is particularly important for dense boundary parsing with the smaller ViT-S, yielding the highest foreground IoU of 70.04%70.04\%. In contrast, LEF-JEPA-CIM casts local correction as a combinatorial low-energy search on a physical CIM: discrete spin couplings naturally filter fine-grained local texture and color fluctuations, directly providing a region-level consistency constraint. Consequently, with a single local update (K=1K=1), LEF-JEPA-CIM efficiently guides the encoder, attaining the strongest global classification and spatial planning results on both backbones. On ViT-B, LEF-JEPA-CIM further outperforms LEF-JEPA and achieves the highest foreground IoU of 72.11%72.11\%.

4.3 Ablation Studies

4.3.1 Number of Energy-Gradient Updates

Figure 6 compares the effect of the number of energy-gradient updates K∈{1,3,5}K\in\{1,3,5\} on pretraining latency and downstream transfer. Even with a single update (K=1K=1), both energy realizations improve segmentation and planning over the energy-free V-JEPA2 baseline. For continuous neural energy, K=3K=3 attains the highest foreground IoU on both backbones and provides a more balanced cross-task profile; increasing to K=5K=5 further improves classification accuracy but does not further improve segmentation or planning performance.

In contrast, LEF-JEPA-CIM favors a shallower update depth: K=1K=1 gives the best results on all three tasks for ViT-B, while classification and planning are likewise best at K=1K=1 for ViT-S. Because the physical CIM is queried only once at the initial state q0q_{0} and subsequent updates reuse the same low-energy spin pool, increasing KK primarily repeats rescoring and yields no consistent gain.

4.3.2 Weight of the Relative-Energy Constraint λenc\lambda_{\mathrm{enc}}

Table 2 compares the effect of different λenc\lambda_{\mathrm{enc}} values on downstream transfer with ViT-S, where LEF-JEPA and LEF-JEPA-CIM use K=3K=3 and K=1K=1, respectively. This coefficient controls the strength of the encoder energy constraint ℒenc\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{enc}} relative to the masked-prediction objective ℒpred\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pred}}.

As shown in Table 2, the task-specific optima do not coincide for continuous energy: λenc=0.005\lambda_{\mathrm{enc}}=0.005 attains the highest foreground IoU while maintaining strong overall performance in classification and planning. For LEF-JEPA-CIM, 10−410^{-4} yields the highest classification accuracy and foreground IoU while retaining 79%79\% planning success. Increasing the coefficient to 0.050.05 raises planning success to 81%81\% but substantially reduces classification and segmentation. Overall, both realizations show clear sensitivity to the constraint strength, and an overly strong relative-energy constraint degrades classification and segmentation performance.

5 Conclusion

This work shows that latent representations for world modeling should not only recover the spatial structure of objects, but also avoid overemphasizing low-level visual information, such as texture and color, that is not always necessary for prediction and action. Through target-guided latent recovery and relative-energy supervision, LEF-JEPA enables frozen representations to benefit jointly across image recognition, cross-domain foreground segmentation, and visual planning without adding downstream inference overhead. Our experiments further show that this energy learning framework can be realized either by a continuous neural network or by coupling a conditional Ising Hamiltonian to a physical CIM; the latter retains strong cross-task performance with a shallow local-update horizon. Overall, the results show that structure learning in latent space need not rely on the pointwise modeling of low-level visual information such as texture and color; instead, local recovery and energy relations can organize the spatial structure required by downstream tasks. Future work will explore the applicability and efficiency of this mechanism in long-video world models and on larger-scale specialized Ising solvers.

Supplementary Material

Appendix A Notation and Optimization Paths

A.1 Symbols

Table S1 collects the main notation used across the neural and Ising energy realizations. The symbol SS denotes the clean online candidate representation, whereas 𝒮\mathcal{S} denotes a finite pool of Ising spin states; the different typefaces are intentional.

A.2 Gradient routing

The two energy objectives share the same conditional energy function but assign it different optimization roles. Table S2 lists the trainable recipients of each loss. The Energy Field Loss treats SS, CC, and TT as fixed and updates only the energy parameters. Its KK-step update graph retains ∇qE\nabla_{q}E, so backpropagation evaluates the required Hessian–vector products involving mixed second-order derivatives with respect to the state and energy parameters, without materializing a full Hessian. The Encoder Energy Loss freezes the energy parameters, the explicit anchor-condition branch, and the target representation. Gradients enter the online encoder through the source branch SS; the shared visible-token centering and RMS statistics used to construct SS couple candidate and anchor positions. This separation prevents the unrolled energy-gradient updates from becoming an additional reconstruction path into the visual encoder.

A.3 Local-roughness visualization

The local-roughness maps in Figure 1 are computed from final-layer patch tokens without training a probe. For each image, we fit PCA independently and retain the first three components. Let zp∈ℝ3z_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} be the projected coordinate at patch position pp, let z~p\tilde{z}_{p} denote its spatially centered value, and define the image-level RMS-normalized coordinate

up=z~p|Ω|−1​∑r∈Ω‖z~r‖22.u_{p}=\frac{\tilde{z}_{p}}{\sqrt{|\Omega|^{-1}\sum_{r\in\Omega}\|\tilde{z}_{r}\|_{2}^{2}}}. (S1)

The local roughness at pp is the mean squared difference to its available horizontal and vertical one-patch neighbors:

R⁡(p)=1|𝒩4​(p)|​∑q∈𝒩4​(p)‖up−uq‖22,R(p)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}_{4}(p)|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{N}_{4}(p)}\|u_{p}-u_{q}\|_{2}^{2}, (S2)

where 𝒩4​(p)\mathcal{N}_{4}(p) contains the valid four-neighborhood positions. Thus, bright responses indicate a stronger local change in the three-dimensional PCA field. All methods use the same fixed visualization range R∈[0,2]R\in[0,2].

A.4 Pretraining hyperparameters

Table S3 summarizes the hyperparameters used in the main pretraining experiments. Batch sizes are per device. The online optimizer jointly updates the visual encoder and masked predictor, while a separate optimizer updates the energy module.

Appendix B Datasets and Task Construction

B.1 CIFAR-10 pretraining and classification

CIFAR-10 contains 50,00050{,}000 training images and 10,00010{,}000 test images from ten object categories, each at 32×3232\times 32 resolution. Encoder parameters are optimized exclusively by self-supervised objectives over the complete CIFAR-10 training split. For hyperparameter selection, we use a fixed 5,000-image subset of the training split as the validation subset and fit a linear classifier on frozen representations from the remaining training images. We select KK and λenc\lambda_{\mathrm{enc}} using the mean top-1 accuracy of three independently pretrained encoders on the validation subset. The selected hyperparameters are then fixed for all subsequent downstream evaluations. The online and target encoders receive the same augmented view. Augmentation comprises reflection-padded random cropping, horizontal flipping, and mild color jitter, applied with probabilities 0.50.5, 0.50.5, and 0.20.2, respectively. Within each encoder scale, all methods use the same augmentation, masking distribution, and number of pretraining epochs.

B.2 PartImageNet foreground transfer

PartImageNet provides dense part annotations for general object categories. The evaluation converts its whole-object annotation into a binary foreground/background target. The local release contains 20,46620{,}466 training, 1,2061{,}206 validation, and 2,4082{,}408 test images. Images and masks are resized to 32×3232\times 32 using bilinear and nearest-neighbor interpolation, respectively. A patch is labeled foreground when at least half of its pixels belong to the annotated object. This conversion gives a 16×1616\times 16 target grid for a patch size of two pixels. The encoder remains frozen and only a shared 1×11\times 1 two-class convolution is fitted over its final patch features.

B.3 Two-Room visual planning

Two-Room is a controlled 65×6565\times 65 environment containing an agent and a vertical wall with a traversable opening. Observations contain separate agent and wall channels. The image adapter renders these channels as RGB, resizes the result to 32×3232\times 32.

Each predictor step consumes a block of five consecutive two-dimensional primitive actions. Training unrolls eight such blocks, corresponding to 4040 primitive actions and nine latent states. Evaluation is open loop. Start and goal states are sampled as random pairs, and success is declared when the Euclidean state distance falls below 4.54.5 environment units.

Appendix C Architecture and Pretraining Details

The baselines are V-JEPA2 as the direct no-energy control, EB-JEPA retrained through its official repository, and V-JEPA2.1 retrained from its open-source implementation under the same settings.

C.1 Network architecture and target representations

The masked region is the union of eleven or twelve overlapping 4×44\times 4 blocks, calibrated to an average masking ratio of approximately 50%50\%. Visible positions are partitioned into candidate and anchor subsets at a 1:11{:}1 ratio using block-based spatial sampling, while retaining their original grid coordinates.

The target encoder is initialized from the online encoder and updated by EMA. Its momentum follows a cosine schedule from 0.9960.996 to 0.99950.9995, and target tokens are normalized without learnable affine parameters. The anchor condition uses online layers 6 and 9 with weights (0.5,0.5)(0.5,0.5); the target reference combines target layers 6, 9, and 12 with weights (0.25,0.25,0.5)(0.25,0.25,0.5). Each layer is spatially centered and RMS-normalized before fusion, and the fused target representation is normalized once more.

Candidate features and each anchor level are projected from the encoder width to 160 dimensions. Each energy block contains candidate self-attention, cross-attention from candidate queries to the anchor keys and values, and an MLP. The two anchor levels extract conditional information separately before their outputs are fused. For LEF-JEPA, a shared scalar head is applied to the final normalized candidate features, and its position-wise contributions are summed to produce the conditional energy.

Appendix D Conditional Ising and Physical CIM Implementation

D.1 Coefficient network and differentiable rescoring

The Ising realization first uses B=16B=16 learned queries to extract descriptors ri∈ℝ160r_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{160} for 16 logical spins from the candidate tokens. Each descriptor predicts a unary spin bias hih_{i} and is paired with the other spin descriptors to predict couplings Ji​jJ_{ij}, yielding an Ising Hamiltonian conditioned on the current visual representation.

Concretely, each rir_{i} is projected to a 64-dimensional vector vi=Wp​riv_{i}=W_{p}r_{i}. For every spin pair (i,j)(i,j), viv_{i} and vjv_{j} form the symmetric descriptor

ui​j=[vi+vj,|vi−vj|,vi⊙vj]u_{ij}=\left[v_{i}+v_{j},\;|v_{i}-v_{j}|,\;v_{i}\odot v_{j}\right] (S3)

A shared Pair MLP maps ui​ju_{ij} to the coupling Ji​jJ_{ij} using LayerNorm, 192→64192\rightarrow 64, GELU, and 64→164\rightarrow 1. Because ui​j=uj​iu_{ij}=u_{ji}, its output satisfies Ji​j=Jj​iJ_{ij}=J_{ji}; the diagonal is set to zero.

Hardware-returned spin candidates are detached, rescored with the original floating-point Hamiltonian coefficients, and aggregated into a conditional energy using the truncated soft minimum defined in the main paper. Gradients therefore pass through the coefficient network to the representation, but not through the discrete search process.

D.2 Hardware queries and timing

Physical runs access QBoson’s CIM through the Kaiwu SDK. Each 16-spin logical Hamiltonian is augmented with one reference spin, scaled by a detached positive factor, and quantized to signed integers in [−127,127][-127,127]. Up to 58 such 17-spin blocks are packed into one block-diagonal task, keeping each submission within the 1000-spin hardware limit. Sampling mode returns ten complete readouts of the packed system and therefore ten candidates for every 16-spin Ising subproblem. After reference-spin decoding, candidates are ranked under the submitted quantized Hamiltonian and deduplicated; up to eight distinct low-energy states form the candidate pool.

Each local recovery trajectory queries its pool at the initial state q0q_{0} and reuses it across all KK updates; the coefficients are still recomputed and rescored at every current state qkq_{k}.

All reported LEF-JEPA-CIM results use the physical solver. Pretraining forward timing includes energy-network computation, coefficient preparation, physical solving, and local Hamiltonian and state processing, but excludes network transmission, service queueing, and result-return latency.

Appendix E Frozen Evaluation Protocols

Within each backbone size, all methods use identically structured task heads and matched optimization protocols; only the pretrained weights of the frozen encoder differ.

All reported means and standard deviations aggregate three independently pretrained encoders. Each pretraining seed controls the initialization of the encoder and energy module, minibatch order, data augmentation, masking, and candidate–anchor sampling. Downstream heads use a fixed initialization and data order with the same optimization protocol for every encoder; the reported seed variation therefore reflects encoder pretraining rather than downstream head randomness.

E.1 Classification and foreground segmentation

All downstream evaluations freeze the EMA target encoder. For CIFAR-10 classification, final-layer patch tokens are spatially averaged, and the resulting image-level features are standardized with training-set statistics before fitting a linear classifier. The classifier is trained for 300 epochs with AdamW and a cosine learning-rate schedule; accuracy is aggregated over the three independently pretrained encoders.

For PartImageNet, final-layer patch tokens are cached and used to train a shared linear 1×11\times 1 foreground head for 100 epochs. Test-set foreground IoU is aggregated over the three independently pretrained encoders. Dataset splits and foreground-label construction are described in Section B.

E.2 Two-Room visual planning

Every method uses the same trajectories to train an identically structured action-conditioned latent predictor. The predictor has two Transformer blocks and eight attention heads, with the same width as the frozen encoder. Its training objective combines one-step teacher forcing with an eight-block recursive rollout.

Planning uses a horizon of eight latent blocks, corresponding to 40 primitive actions. CEM performs 30 iterations over 300 candidates and retains 30 elites. Candidate plans are ranked by the mean-squared error between terminal patch tokens and the target representation. Evaluation is open loop. Each pretrained encoder is evaluated on 100 episodes under the same environment-generation protocol, and success rate is averaged across the three encoder runs.

Appendix F Number of Energy-Gradient Updates

Figure S1 and Table S5 examine how the pretraining denoising horizon K∈{1,3,5}K\in\{1,3,5\} affects pretraining latency and downstream transfer. The main experiments use K=3K=3 for LEF-JEPA and K=1K=1 for LEF-JEPA-CIM. Because the energy module is removed after pretraining, KK does not affect deployment latency. For LEF-JEPA-CIM, each recovery trajectory queries the physical solver only once at q0q_{0} and reuses the returned state pool in subsequent updates.

For continuous-energy LEF-JEPA, K=3K=3 gives the highest foreground IoU on both backbones. Increasing the horizon to K=5K=5 further improves classification but does not further improve segmentation or planning performance.

The physical-Ising realization favors a shallower update. At K=1K=1, ViT-B achieves its best result on all three tasks; for ViT-S, classification and planning are also strongest at K=1K=1, while foreground IoU peaks at K=3K=3. Later updates repeatedly rescore the same state pool rather than invoking a new physical search, which is consistent with the absence of systematic gains beyond the first update. The measured K=1K=1 forward latency is approximately 4545–4747 ms, below neural LEF-JEPA at K=3K=3.

Bold in Table S5 marks the best depth for each method, backbone, and task.
